public_payload.normalized_proposition: AI agents will require common sense about objects, people, and entities to work reliably in the real world.
conditions: working reliably in the real world, not just as demos

statement.excerpt: Making them work reliably in the real world — and not just as demos - will require common sense – about objects, people, and entities in the world.
statement.document_title: AI still lacks “common” sense, 70 years later

from_speaker: Making them work reliably in the real world
about objects, people, and entities in the world
our_interpretation: The claim states a necessary condition: agents that work reliably in real-world use must possess relevant commonsense competence.
I read reliability as consistently completing the tasks entrusted to the agent under ordinary operational variation. It does not mean flawless performance or competence at every possible task.

I read common sense as practical understanding of relevant entities, their properties and identities, and the implications of ordinary interactions. Competence must be assessed separately from overall task success to avoid circular reasoning.
The claim requires possessing competence, not a recognized research advance, a particular architecture, or evidence about how that competence developed.
Human oversight does not automatically disqualify a deployment, but human corrections must be distinguished from the agent's own reliable performance.
The antecedent is established reliable real-world operation. Deployment alone, relative improvement, and simulated workplace evaluations do not establish it.
criteria.support_condition: After reliable real-world operation is established, evaluations of those same agents demonstrate relevant commonsense competence across the situations encountered in deployment. Consistent findings across deployments would support the claim within the tested scope, although coexistence alone cannot conclusively establish universal necessity.
criteria.contradiction_condition: An agent consistently performs real-world tasks involving relevant objects, people, or entities, while separate, valid evaluations establish that it lacks the commonsense competence those situations call for. Its reliability must not be attributable to humans supplying the missing judgments.

evidence.publisher: Pan et al., arXiv; accepted at ICML 2026
evidence.explanation: The study collected deployment evidence from April through November 2025. It documents practical approaches to reliability, but does not independently establish sustained agent performance and separately measure the relevant commonsense competence.

The evaluation identifies failures relevant to Marcus's account of commonsense competence. Its simulated e-commerce tasks neither establish reliable real-world deployment nor show that such competence is universally necessary.

This is evidence of improvement in actual deployment. A relative improvement does not establish an absolute reliability standard, and the reported result does not test whether the agent lacks relevant commonsense competence.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Operational records establishing consistent real-world performance, paired with separate commonsense tests of the same deployed agent. Reliable performance despite demonstrated absence of relevant competence would refute the claim; competence across reliable deployments would provide scoped support.
